entries.name: Diamond
entries.weathers_to: does not weather; survives to concentrate in alluvial gravels
entries.notes: Hardest natural material. Gem diamonds come from pipes mined open-cast then underground; the carbon itself crystallized 150-250 km down. Worth a deep ore the player cannot reach early.

entries.name: Ruby
entries.notes: Chromium is what separates red ruby from sapphire; fine stones come from Mogok in Myanmar and Montepuez in Mozambique. A red gem rarer and pricier per carat than most diamonds.

entries.name: Sapphire
entries.notes: Any corundum that is not red; blue comes from iron and titanium. Famous sources: Kashmir, Sri Lanka, Montana, Madagascar. Resists scratching; survives transport in rivers.

entries.name: Emerald
entries.weathers_to: concentrates in alluvial gravels, though it fractures before it weathers
entries.notes: Nearly always included and oiled: a flawless emerald is a laboratory stone. Colombia (Muzo) sets the price; Zambia and Brazil follow. Brittle along cleavage despite the beryl family's fame.

entries.name: Amethyst
entries.weathers_to: releases quartz sand with iron staining
entries.notes: The purple is iron plus irradiation; it fades in strong sunlight. Huge geodes line the lava flow walls of Brazil and Uruguay. The everyday purple gem.

entries.name: Rock crystal
entries.notes: Clear quartz: the original 'crystal' of antiquity, used for lenses, seals and ritual objects. Piezoelectric; it still resonates inside watches and radios.

entries.name: Topaz
entries.notes: Most blue topaz on the market is irradiated and heated colorless stone. Imperial topaz (orange-pink) from Ouro Preto in Brazil is the natural prize. Perfect basal cleavage makes it chippy to cut.

entries.name: Opal
entries.weathers_to: crazes and cracks as it dries out
entries.notes: Play of color is diffraction from stacked silica spheres, not pigment. Australia produces ~95% of it; Ethiopia and Mexico follow. Contains up to 20% water; it can craze if it dries.

entries.name: Turquoise
entries.weathers_to: crumbles to clay; color fades with heat and oils
entries.notes: Copper makes the blue, iron the green. Worked for 6000 years in Egypt, Persia and the American Southwest. Soft and porous: it takes polish beautifully and stains just as easily.

entries.name: Garnet (almandine-pyrope)
entries.weathers_to: concentrates in alluvial gravels; also used as garnet sand
entries.notes: A family, not a species: almandine, pyrope, spessartine, tsavorite and more. The workhorse red gem of history, from Viking beads to Noah's-ark-era jewelry, and a common waterjet abrasive.

entries.name: Tourmaline (elbaite)
entries.notes: The most chemically varied gem family: every color, often several in one crystal (watermelon). Paraiba's neon copper-blue comes from a single deposit in Brazil. Strongly pleochroic; large crystals are common.

entries.name: Aquamarine
entries.notes: Beryl colored sky-blue to sea-green by iron; the name is literally 'water of the sea'. Big clean crystals are routine, so size does not equal value. Minas Gerais, Brazil is the classic source.

entries.name: Peridot
entries.notes: The gem variety of olivine, one of the most abundant minerals in Earth's mantle but rare at the surface. Apaches called it the 'evening emerald'; Arizona and China supply the market.

entries.name: Zircon
entries.weathers_to: survives to beach 'zircon sands'; a major zirconium ore
entries.notes: Not cubic zirconia: a real mineral and the best tool for dating rocks (uranium-lead). Some grains are over 4 billion years old. Blue gem zircon is heat-treated; natural is brown.

entries.name: Jadeite
entries.notes: The jade of China and imperial Burma: formed only in subduction zones, often with the legendary chromium green. Tougher than steel to strike, though softer than quartz; worked by grinding and sanding, never carving.

entries.name: Nephrite
entries.notes: The 'jade' of New Zealand (pounamu), Canada and ancient China: an interlocking-fiber felt that will not shatter. Carved objects and heirlooms; the toughest common gem material on Earth.

entries.name: Lapis lazuli
entries.weathers_to: calcite leaches out; pyrite may rust the surface brown
entries.notes: Ground to make ultramarine, worth more than gold for Renaissance paint. Mined in Afghanistan (Sar-e-Sang) for over 6000 years; flecks of pyrite are desirable, calcite white is not.

entries.name: Malachite
entries.weathers_to: dissolves in acidic water; stains soil green
entries.notes: Banded green copper carbonate; the big Russian palaces are faced with it. Soft, silky-banded and toxic if inhaled as dust: cut with water, never dry-grind. A good surface marker for copper ore below.

entries.name: Azurite
entries.weathers_to: alters to malachite in contact with moist air
entries.notes: The deep blue partner of malachite; in damp conditions it slowly turns green. Mixed azurite-malachite 'azure-malachite' stones are common and attractive. Medieval painters paid dearly for well-crystallized blue.

entries.name: Amber
entries.weathers_to: survives in sediments; burns with a resinous lavender flame
entries.notes: Not a mineral at all: 30-90 million year old pine resin, famous for trapped insects. Baltic amber washed up on North Sea shores; floats in salt water, sinks in fresh. Soft enough to scratch with a fingernail.

entries.name: Pearl
entries.weathers_to: nacre dissolves in weak acids; layers can peel
entries.notes: The only gem grown inside a living animal; concentric nacre around an irritant. Natural pearls are among the rarest gems by value; cultured akoya, South Sea and freshwater supply the market. Vinegar will destroy one.

entries.name: Moonstone
entries.notes: The adularescent glow is light scattered between microscopic layers of two feldspars. Fine blue-sheen stones come from Sri Lanka and Myanmar; rainbow moonstone is a labradorite relative from India. Roman-era gem.

entries.name: Labradorite
entries.weathers_to: feldspar weathers to clay; iridescence dies with it
entries.notes: Gray-blue base with flashes of peacock green and electric blue (labradorescence). Named after Labrador, Canada; Finnish 'spectrolite' shows the full spectrum. Whole cliffs of it feature in monumental architecture.

entries.name: Citrine
entries.notes: Natural citrine is rare; nearly all commercial 'citrine' is heat-treated amethyst or smoky quartz. November's birthstone. The Madeira-orange saturated stones are the most valued.

entries.name: Rose quartz
entries.notes: Milky pink from microscopic inclusions; large gemmy crystals are rare and usually cloudy. The workhorse of crystal shops and mass-market bracelets. Fades in constant sun.

entries.name: Smoky quartz
entries.notes: Aluminium color centers darkened by natural irradiation; fully black stones are 'morion'. The Swiss Alps yield huge museum-grade crystals. Scarab amulets in Egypt were cut from it.

entries.name: Tiger's eye
entries.notes: Quartz replacing asbestos fibers, preserving the silky chatoyant bands. South Africa dominates the supply. The blue-grey parent is 'hawk's eye'; heating turns it red-brown ('bull's eye').

entries.name: Chrysoprase
entries.weathers_to: loses color as it dries; recovers with moisture
entries.notes: Apple-green nickel-colored chalcedony, Frederick the Great's favorite gem (he had entire rooms faced with it). Australian deposits at Marlborough and Turkey's Eskisehir dominate. Color fades when dehydrated.

entries.name: Morganite
entries.notes: Pink beryl colored by manganese; named for banker J.P. Morgan in 1910. Brazil and Madagascar produce large clean stones. Peach tones are the most prized; big stones are often pale.

entries.name: Chrysoberyl
entries.notes: Third hardest natural gem after diamond and corundum; 'cat's eye' (cymophane) shows a single sharp fiber band. Named for gold-white color, unrelated to beryl despite both holding beryllium.

entries.name: Alexandrite
entries.notes: The color-change phenomenon: green in daylight, red in incandescent light, from a narrow chromium absorption window. Named for the future Tsar Alexander II; original Ural stones are nearly gone. Lab-grown is common, natural is precious.

entries.name: Spinel
entries.notes: For centuries confused with ruby: the Black Prince's and Timur rubies in the British Crown Jewels are red spinels. Flame-orange and cobalt-blue stones are newly fashionable. Single refraction, unlike corundum.

entries.name: Iolite
entries.notes: Vikings may have used it as a polarizing filter (sunstone) to locate the sun under overcast skies. Strongly pleochroic: violet-blue, grey, pale yellow depending on the angle. Lisbon-era sailors' navigation aid.

entries.name: Tanzanite
entries.weathers_to: concentrates in residual soils at the mine
entries.notes: Found in a single 7x2 km field near Kilimanjaro in 1967, ever since mined under a Tanzanian government monopoly. Strong trichroism: blue, violet, burgundy. Most rough is heat-treated to kill the brown veil.

entries.name: Benitoite
entries.notes: California's state gem; sapphire-blue and strongly dispersive, fluorescing bright blue under short-wave UV. Gem material comes from one creek bed in San Benito County. A genuinely scarce 'California sapphire'.

entries.name: Taaffeite
entries.notes: The only gem first identified from a cut stone: Count Taaffe spotted it in a Dublin jeweler's tray in 1945, mislabeled as spinel. A million times rarer than diamond. Double refraction gives it away.

entries.name: Painite
entries.notes: Long listed in the Guinness Book as the world's rarest mineral: only a handful of crystals known for decades after 1954. Hundreds more surfaced near Mogok after 2000. Brownish-red, near topaz in looks.
